content: In the youngest age group, consuming unfortified foods in practical amounts can meet all target nutrient requirements except for iron during infancy. However, this is only achievable if there is access to a wide variety of foods from all food groups, including diverse vegetables and protein subgroups, and if these foods are consumed regularly. When certain food groups or subgroups are excluded, significant nutrient deficiencies arise. For example, at 9 months of age, eliminating whole grains, vegetables, or specific protein subgroups leads to multiple nutrient gaps. While no additional gaps for target nutrients were observed in some scenarios, the iron deficiency gap worsened. In other cases, deficiencies in iron, vitamin B12, or vitamin C were noted. The exclusion of all fruits and vegetables, all flesh foods, or all animal-source foods was particularly problematic for older infants and young children (IYC). When staple foods are monotonous or their quantities are increased, multiple nutrient gaps also occur in the youngest age group. However, for older IYC, no additional nutrient gaps were observed if the diet included diverse, nutrient-dense foods in optimal patterns. Introducing unhealthy foods or beverages into the diet of 9-month-old infants leaves no room for these items without compromising nutrient intake. However, for older IYC, there is some dietary flexibility to include a daily serving of unhealthy foods, provided the diet also includes diverse, nutrient-dense foods. When real-world food patterns are approximated, gaps in B vitamins, choline, and minerals are observed across all settings, with more severe and numerous deficiencies in countries like Bangladesh and Malawi. These gaps are larger compared to those seen in idealized model solutions. Fortified items can partially address nutrient gaps, but their effectiveness varies depending on their composition and energy content. For the youngest infants, products like small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) and Super Cereal Plus displaced most foods other than breast milk, leading to nutrient gaps. However, in modeled food patterns, all fortified products reduced gaps for vitamin D, with SQ-LNS and micronutrient powders (MNPs) being particularly effective in reducing or eliminating iron deficiencies. SQ-LNS also addressed gaps in zinc, copper, and calcium. Despite these benefits, some nutrient gaps remained in all settings. In conclusion, except for iron and for the youngest infants, it is possible to meet all target nutrient needs through unfortified foods consumed in feasible quantities. However, the ideal food patterns required to achieve this are significantly different from those observed in many real-world settings. For the youngest infants, optimal food patterns include minimal starchy staples. For all IYC, the best dietary patterns are rich in diverse vegetables, include flesh foods, and exclude refined grains. Real-world food patterns often have lower energy contributions from vegetables and protein foods, resulting in numerous nutrient gaps. Fortified items provide only a partial solution to these deficiencies.
